note: Number columns are accounting conventions, never people: no commentator produced a number for this population. The authors section is text: what each argues, what the claim is about, the convention in this ledger that comes closest (if any) and why it is not the same thing. External links live in sources.json, keyed to the ids used here.

presets.label: CBO-informed central case
presets.summary: School spending follows enrollment 63-66%, colleges and other services fully, roads and parks not at all. Defense, general government, interest on existing debt and business subsidies are held fixed. The gain from the group's work is counted.
presets.scope_note: Only two inputs rest on CBO: the rules for who bears each tax, and the school figure, which this repo derives from a CBO regression. Holding defense, general government and interest at zero is this account's assumption. The column "Central case, general government grows with the population" tests the general-government part.

settings.label: School spending
settings.note: CBO's state panel: spending per pupil grows 0.37 points slower for each point of enrollment growth, and 0.34 points faster for each point of decline. Total school spending then moves 63-66% as much as enrollment. These are two point values; the range covers both.

settings.label: School spending, both values
settings.note: Both values enter the range of open choices.

settings.label: College and other education
settings.note: The account's profile cbo_category_lag_non_school_full. Holding this at zero instead gives 121-160 bn.

misses: Second-generation and lifetime dynamics: this is one income year of a population already here.
Any cost specific to crime: police, courts and prisons are charged per head.
Prices, elder care and gains from complementary skills beyond the production model (see "Objections, with the result this repo computed for each"; none of them can be added).

presets.label: Central case, general government grows with the population
presets.summary: The central case, except that general government is no longer fixed. Tax collection, financial management and state and local administration grow with the population; legislatures and the federal executive do not. Defense and interest on debt already issued stay fixed.
presets.scope_note: Raised on 2026-09-21. 63% of general government outside interest is state and local, and across the 50 states administration spending rises 8.4% for every 10% more residents. That is long-run evidence about scale, not a measured response to this group.

settings.label: General government
settings.note: The low end of the implied range: the federal executive and legislature held fixed, federal tax collection and all state and local administration growing as they do across states.
settings.ref: assumption_explorer_2026_09_21/scaling_check.py; BEA Table 3.16 lines 3-6 and 44-47; Census 2022 State and Local Government Finance, Table 1

misses: A causal estimate. A comparison across states shows how administration scales in the long run, not what one group's presence adds.
Federal police, courts and prisons (82.8 bn, the FBI among them) are not here: they were already charged, inside police, courts and prisons.

presets.label: All services at average cost
presets.summary: Every public service grows one for one with the population. This is the account's proportional benchmark, 270-289 bn.
misses: Evidence that school budgets move less than one for one with enrollment in the short run (63-66%, derived from CBO).

presets.label: Taxes paid minus benefits received
presets.summary: The common tally: what the group pays in taxes against the cash and in-kind benefits it draws. No schools, no police, no production side.

settings.label: Public services
settings.note: A tally of taxes against benefits never charges services.

settings.label: Gain from the group's work
settings.note: A budget tally has no production side.

misses: Education: about 200 bn assigned to this group, the largest single line in the ledger.
Police, courts, health and other services: about 158 bn.
The gain from the group's work, which a budget tally also leaves out.

presets.label: No public services charged
presets.summary: Taxes, benefits and the gain from the group's work, with schools, police, health and every other service left out. This is the nearest this combined federal, state and local ledger comes to a federal-budget view, because federal agencies deliver 1% of education and 15% of police, courts and prisons.
presets.scope_note: It is not a federal-only account: state and local taxes are still counted here. A true federal window would drop them too.
misses: Every service line: 358 bn assigned to the group, 200 bn of it education.
CBO's own state and local report: for the surge population, costs exceeded revenues by 9.2 bn in 2023.

presets.label: Everything at average cost
presets.summary: A per-head share of every line, including defense, general government and interest on debt already issued, and no gain from the group's work.

settings.label: Interest on existing debt
settings.note: Charged per head, although debt already issued does not shrink with the population.

misses: Defense and interest on existing debt do not fall when a population is smaller, and about 237 bn of this total is spending of that kind.
The gain to other residents from the group's work.
Evidence that school budgets move 63-66% as much as enrollment, not 100%.

presets.label: Production side only
presets.summary: No budget lines at all: only what other residents gain privately from the group's work. Once investment has caught up, this account's production model leaves almost nothing for other residents directly. What remains arrives as extra tax receipts on the added output, and a view with no budget lines drops those too.
presets.scope_note: The production model has constant returns by construction. Arguments from increasing returns (ideas, specialization, fixed costs) cannot be represented in it.
misses: Every fiscal line: taxes, benefits and services.

standing.title: Whose ledger is this?
rows: This page. The taxes the group pays, the benefits and services it draws, and the gain from its work that reaches everyone else.
What they earn here against what they would earn elsewhere, known as the place premium. It is inside US GDP but not in this ledger, and it is where most of any world-GDP gain sits.
Effects on countries of origin: money sent home, workers departed.
standing.text: Claims about world GDP add all three. They cannot be netted against this page's number without deciding how much a dollar to a migrant counts against a dollar to someone already here, which is a moral weight, not a measurement. Interest on US debt would never be deducted from world GDP: it is a payment from taxpayers to bondholders, a transfer, and no output is lost. Inside this ledger it is held fixed because debt already issued does not shrink when a population is smaller.

authors.name: Noah Smith
argues: He cites CBO's July 2024 projection: the 2021-26 surge lowers covered federal deficits by about $0.9tn over 2024-2034. CBO's headline excludes discretionary appropriations and state and local budgets.

In his own words the same arrivals are "a long-term fiscal problem, because these people will require heavy government support for their health care, housing, and education; this will end up coming from city and state governments".
authors.object: A recent surge of all origins, the federal budget, a ten-year window.

closest.why: A claim about the federal budget does not charge schools or police, which are almost entirely state and local. He names that local cost himself and does not net it against the federal gain. The repo's September revision no longer calls this a contradiction.

leaves_out: The second generation: 'no mention of the second generation' (scorecard :35). Most of this population is US-born.
A number for the gain from production or complementary skills: none is recorded.

authors.name: Matthew Yglesias
argues: He states no fiscal number in his own voice. The CBO material on Slow Boring is in guest posts (Kolko, 2024-09-12; Elmendorf and Williams, 2023-08-28).

His case is scale and growth, lower grocery and service prices, and hours freed for high-wage women. On cost he has one aside, in a sentence about housing: the tools to end housing shortages, "like immigration", "would cost taxpayers nothing". He concedes congestion costs (traffic, rent, water, pollution) and that crime counts rise with population.
authors.object: Immigrants 'of virtually all stripes', national scale, no stated horizon.

closest.why: This is the condition under which immigration "would cost taxpayers nothing" holds in this ledger. That is an inference from his aside; he did not argue it. His price channel is outside the account (see the objections section).

leaves_out: Local budgets: 'He addresses wages, not local budgets' (audit :67).
The National Academies 2016 report, and any federal, Social Security or debt number of his own (audit :138-139).

authors.name: Bryan Caplan
argues: A moral presumption in favor of free migration, and an economic case that is 'extremely strong': very large global gains from moving labor to productive places. The 'double world GDP' figure is sourced to openborders.info, not to a sentence of his.
Restrictions 'are not necessary to protect American taxpayers': fiscal effects are modest, and where they are not, cheaper keyhole remedies exist (entry fees, surtaxes, exclusion from benefits).
authors.object: Future entrants under open borders; the welfare of migrants and the world as well as natives.

closest.why: No setting of this ledger represents his claim, so no number is shown. His large gains accrue mainly to the migrants themselves (the second row of the table above), and his keyhole remedy applies to future entrants: it cannot be applied to a resident population that is mostly US-born citizens. Switching benefits off in this ledger would only stop counting 364 bn of costs; it would not be his argument.

leaves_out: School, shelter and service load on state and local budgets: what survives an exclusion from welfare (audit :288). The audit's verdict on the taxpayer claim: 'Federal gains can coexist with state/local costs in education, shelter, and related services'.
The cost and feasibility of the keyhole instruments themselves (audit :216).

authors.name: Nicholas Decker
argues: 'Immigrants must make us richer': "I think the assumption of constant returns to scale is nonsense. Not only that, it is obvious nonsense… There are three main channels by which returns simply have to be increasing: specialization, ideas, and fixed costs… of course immigrants make us richer."
authors.object: All immigrants; the total income of people already here; no horizon or cost convention stated.

closest.why: His argument has a production side and no fiscal side. But this ledger's production model has constant returns, the assumption he rejects, so its near-zero private gain is this account's result and not a test of his claim. The repo has withdrawn two of its own earlier rebuttals of him.

leaves_out: Every fiscal line: the audits record him compressing the question into 'one production-function dispute' (audit 2026-04-11 :255-256).
Composition: his July 2026 proposal to rank visas concedes that composition decides the sign (scorecard :79).
